title: When does the epigenetic clock get your age wrong, and why?
bullets: Team Neural Ninjas · AI and Visualization Lab WS26, JKU Linz
Phase I progress update (midpoint)
Pair A (with GenAI): Ali Haider Warraich · Carola Gödeke
Pair B (without GenAI): Abrar Ahmad · Haseeb Ahmed
narration: Hi, we are team Neural Ninjas: Ali Haider Warraich, Carola Gödeke, Abrar Ahmad and Haseeb Ahmed. This is our Phase One progress update on the question: when does the epigenetic clock get your age wrong, and why?

title: The problem
bullets: DNA methylation changes steadily with age
Epigenetic clocks: pre-trained linear models, weighted sum of CpG methylation (beta values) → age
Models under investigation: Horvath (2013) and Hannum (2013)
RQ1: For whom are the clocks wrong? Bias or random error?
RQ2: How stable are predictions under noise and missing CpGs?
Hypothesis: the clocks underestimate very old people
narration: Epigenetic clocks are pre-trained linear models that read DNA methylation at a few hundred CpG sites and estimate a person's age. We investigate two published clocks, Horvath and Hannum, first as black boxes. Research question one: for whom are the clocks wrong, and is the error systematic? Research question two: how stable are the predictions under noise and missing CpGs? Our hypothesis: the clocks underestimate very old people.

title: Data and models
bullets: GSE40279 (GEO): 656 people, whole blood, Illumina 450K
Age 19–101 · sex · ethnicity · 9 processing plates
Horvath: 353 CpGs, multi-tissue, age-transformed output
Hannum: 71 CpGs, blood; trained on this very dataset (in-sample, optimistic)
narration: Our dataset is GSE40279: 656 people aged 19 to 101, whole blood, Illumina 450K array, with sex, ethnicity and processing plate. Horvath uses 353 CpGs from many tissues. Hannum uses 71 CpGs and was trained on this very dataset, so its results here are optimistic.

title: Pipeline and verification
bullets: Stream the 1.2 GB series matrix → keep the 418 clock CpGs
0 missing values → nothing imputed
Both clocks applied in Python with the published weights
Cross-check with the official methylclock R package: identical for all 656 people (max difference 0.0000 years)
Perturbation test: Gaussian noise and missing CpGs, 20 draws per setting
narration: We keep the 418 clock CpGs from the 1.2 gigabyte matrix; no values were missing. We apply both clocks in Python and cross-checked them against the official methylclock R package: identical for all 656 people. For research question two, we add noise or remove CpGs, twenty times per setting.

title: Pair A (with GenAI): interactive Phase I view
bullets: Predicted vs. real age, one dot per person
Filters: clock, sex, ethnicity, age range
Noise and missing-CpG sliders recompute both clocks live
Error by age, stability chart, metrics per group
narration: Pair A, Ali and Carola, worked with generative AI and built this interactive view. Each dot is one person, predicted against real age. Filters for clock, sex, ethnicity and age range update everything live. The noise and missing CpG sliders recompute both clocks directly in the browser, and a summary table breaks the error down by age band, sex, ethnicity or plate.

title: Finding 1: the error depends on age
bullets: Both clocks lose ~2 years per decade
Half of the over-80s off by > 8 y (Horvath)
Systematic bias, not random error → hypothesis supported
narration: Finding one: the error depends on age. Both clocks lose about two years per decade. They overestimate young people and underestimate old people. For the Horvath clock, the mean error goes from plus two years for people under forty to minus seven and a half years for people over eighty, where half of all people are off by more than eight years. This is systematic bias, not random noise, and it supports our hypothesis.

title: Finding 2: Hannum overestimates almost everyone
bullets: Hannum bias +4.7 y overall, despite in-sample data
Identical in methylclock → real clock behaviour, not a bug
Looks best at 80+ only because the offset cancels the old-age underestimate
Men: +6.0 y vs. women: +3.6 y
narration: Finding two: the Hannum clock overestimates almost everyone, by about 4.7 years on average, even though it was trained on this data. Because methylclock gives exactly the same numbers, this is how the published clock behaves, not a bug in our code. Hannum looks good for the oldest group only because its offset cancels the old-age underestimate. It also overestimates men more than women.

title: Finding 3: batch effect, confounded with age
bullets: Plates differ in mean age (39–76 y)
All Hispanic participants on plates 5, 6, 9
Raw plate differences are mostly age
After removing the age trend: ±3 y batch effect remains
narration: Finding three: at first, the processing plates look like a big source of error. But plates are confounded with age and ethnicity. All Hispanic participants are on three plates, and the mean age per plate ranges from 39 to 76. After removing the age trend, a batch effect of about plus or minus three years remains.

title: Finding 4: stability (RQ2)
bullets: Realistic array noise (SD 0.01–0.02): error grows < 1 y
More noise: Horvath degrades ~2× faster than Hannum
Reason: larger weights, ×21 in the age transformation
Missing CpGs hurt both clocks equally
narration: Finding four is about stability. At realistic array noise the clocks are robust, and the error grows by less than one year. With more noise, the Horvath clock degrades about twice as fast as Hannum, because its weights are larger and are multiplied by twenty-one when converted to years. Missing CpGs hurt both clocks about equally.

title: Pair B (without GenAI): independent findings
bullets: Abrar Ahmad · Haseeb Ahmed — ran the full pipeline without AI assistance
Horvath MAE 4.8 y vs Hannum MAE 5.5 y; Hannum systematically overestimates by +4.7 y
Clear age gradient: both clocks overestimate <40 and underestimate 80+ (Horvath −7.5 y)
Half of the over-80 group is off by >8 years on Horvath — supports the saturation hypothesis
Hannum sex difference: men +6.0 y, women +3.6 y; residual–age correlation ≈ −0.5 for both
narration: Pair B, Abrar and Haseeb, worked without generative AI. They ran the pipeline themselves and confirmed the same core pattern: Horvath has lower overall error, but both clocks show a strong age-dependent bias. Young adults are overestimated, the oldest group is underestimated by about seven and a half years on Horvath, and half of those over eighty are off by more than eight years. Hannum overestimates almost everyone, especially men. The residual-to-age correlation of about minus point five shows the error is systematic, not random.

title: GenAI experience and next steps
bullets: Works best with full context: concept document + course requirements in one prompt
Critical follow-up questions caught a silent substitution (Python instead of methylclock) → led to the cross-check
The AI's own verification script had a bug, caught because the result contradicted other evidence
Phase II: pairs swap; per-CpG contribution waterfall + aging-DNA view to test CpG saturation
narration: Our GenAI lessons: it works best with full context, like our whole concept document. Critical follow-up questions mattered most: asking how it applied methylclock revealed a silent substitution and led to the cross-check. Its own verification script also had a bug, caught because the result contradicted other evidence. In Phase Two the pairs swap, and we open the models with per-CpG contribution waterfalls and an aging DNA view. Thank you.
